Sweet corn is one of the foods that begins converting the sugar to starch as soon as it is picked. That's why the fresher the better. This in fact starts happening within minutes of picking, so if you have a garden with sweet corn, the greatest corn is the cobs that you literally pull off the stalk and then walk in and drop into already boiling salted water.

Peas are another produce that start converting the starch as soon as they are picked, which is why virtually all of the peas in the world are frozen. After just a few days, they've converted a distasteful amount of the sugar into starch, but freezing stops the enzyme that does the conversion.

Another similar thing is tomatoes. There are so many pitiful tomatoes out there for two reasons. First, virtually no tomatoes sold at a supermarket are actually ripe. Ripe tomatoes are too hard to ship, so they are picked at the breaker stage (mix of green and red flesh) and then reddened (not ripened) with chemicals right before they are delivered to the store. "On the vine" tomatoes aren't any better -- they just have vines attached. You need to find "vine ripened" tomatoes -- and good luck with that. If you do, they cost about twice as much, and are worth it.

The other thing about tomatoes is that there is are flavorful volatiles in it them that are destroyed when the temp of the tomato drops below 50 degrees or so, so you should avoid putting ripe tomatoes in the fridge unless that is the only way to keep them from rotting.

Between ripeness and how fast they rot after being picked and how cold damages them, you might be seeing why so many gardeners start with tomatoes. The problem with that is that tomatoes are one of the most frustrating things for gardeners to get a satisfying (if any at all) crop from.

So your number one hunts at the farmers market should be corn, peae, and tomatoes. Those are the three things that supermarkets just can't get right (and it's really not their fault.) Get your corn and peas frozen when not in season (since that locks in the sugar and the freezing plant is often right beside the field) and find someone else to make friends with who is good at growing tomatoes. If they are good at it, they always have fruits to give away. A BLT made with fresh tomatoes and good thick bacon is a bite of heaven.
